newsitem.title: UK: UK budget-need for fiscal tightening questioned.
newsitem.headline: UK budget-need for fiscal tightening questioned.

text.p: The prevailing view that Britain's new Labour government will tighten fiscal policy to dampen demand in its July 2 budget is being challenged by a growing number of economists.

They say taxes will be left broadly unchanged and interest rates -- now the responsibility of the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee -- will instead assume the burden of slowing activity.

Labour's election promise to stick to existing strict departmental spending plans for the next two years rule out fresh spending cuts, while the party also promised not to raise income tax rates or broaden the range of goods subject to value-added tax (VAT).
That still leaves open the option of raising corporate tax and the level of VAT.

But some economists believe this would run against the spirit of the manifesto and, since there is no extraordinary budgetary reason to tighten policy, the government will not risk losing goodwill early in the administration.

"The Labour Party has worked hard to shed the image of the party of high taxation, which involved some explicit promises on income tax ahead of the election," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan. "It is difficult to imagine that its leaders will cast aside these pledges at the first opportunity."
Leading tax firm KPMG this week forecast that VAT would be left unchanged at 17.5 percent in July.

"It is almost beyond belief that a Labour government would raise VAT in its first budget. It is such a regressive tax and was the subject of Labour's key criticism of the outgoing Conservatives," said Ian Barlow, head of tax at KPMG.
Nor is the government likely to tap the corporate sector since it is eager to boost investment, he believes.
"We don't see any change to the 33 percent corporation tax rate, although tax breaks on dividends might be altered."

Labour's manifesto said the centrepiece of the first budget would be a windfall tax on privatised utilities. But since this is ring-fenced to fund a welfare-to-work programme, it does not amount to a policy tightening.

The Conservatives were attacked by Labour during the election campaign for breaking their 1992 promise not to raise taxes. VAT on most goods shot up in 1993 as the Conservatives tried to rein in the public sector borrowing requirement (budget deficit).

But Labour are not going to be able to use that excuse this year. "The PSBR was close to eight percent of GDP in 1993. It was a real crisis and there is no such crisis today. Most expectations are that this year's PSBR will come in at 3.0 percent or below," said Mackie.
Economists from investment bank Goldman Sachs and the respected think-tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) have also ruled out big tax rises.
In their "Green Budget", detailing budget forecasts and analysis, they said higher interest rates would be a more effective way to rein in rampant consumer spending.

"We do not actually think there is a major problem with the budget deficit at the moment," said Goldman Sachs chief economist Gavyn Davies, a close ally of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown who is widely expected to be appointed deputy governor of the Bank of England.

He estimates that a considerable fiscal restraint of around 1.0 percent is already in the pipeline for this tax year, mostly as a result of the tight spending plans, which mean government expenditure will fall well below the economic growth rate.
Economists who favour monetary over fiscal tightening also stress the greater efficiency of higher rates in slowing growth.

The "Green Budget" calculated that personal taxes would have to rise by around nine billion pounds ($14.7 billion) to take the strain off monetary policy sufficiently to allow for a one percentage point cut.

Mackie agrees. "The size of the tax rises needed would be prohibitively large relative to the magnitude of the necessary hike in interest rates. Quite simply, monetary policy is a more effective way of slowing growth and containing inflationary pressures."
But if little or no fiscal tightening is the outcome on July 2, interest rates will have to rise more steeply than financial markets anticipate.
Short sterling futures are factoring in a series of quarter point rises, with rates peaking at around seven percent.
"If monetary policy is to bear the burden of slowing growth rates will have to rise to around 7.5 percent," said Mackie.

The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee meets for the first time today and Friday. A Reuters survey of 21 economists showed a narrow majority anticipating a rate rise, with 12 expecting base rates to rise to 6.5 percent on Friday from the present 6.25 percent.
